'''''Introduction to Commutative Algebra''''' (often informally referred to by the authors' names as "'''Atiyah and Macdonald''"''''') is a well-known [[commutative algebra]] textbook written by [[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Ian G. Macdonald]].<ref>Credited as "I. G. MacDonald" on the cover of ''Introduction to Commutative Algebra'', the author usually spelt his name as "Macdonald" in his other works.</ref> It is on the list of 173 books essential for undergraduate math libraries.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://maa.org/the-basic-library-list-the-basic-library-list-maas-recommendations-for-undergraduate-librariesthe-basic-library-list/ |title=The Basic Library List: MAA's Recommendations for Undergraduate Libraries |access-date=29 July 2026 |website=[[Mathematical Association of America]]}}</ref> As of May 2025, [[Google Scholar]] lists over 8000 citations to this book.

It deals with elementary concepts of commutative algebra including [[localization of a ring|localization]], [[primary decomposition]], [[integrality|integral dependence]], [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] and [[Artinian ring|Artinian]] [[ring (mathematics)|rings]] and [[module (mathematics)|modules]], [[Dedekind ring]]s, [[completion (ring theory)|completions]] and a moderate amount of [[Krull dimension|dimension theory]]. Having originated as a set of lecture notes for third-year undergraduate students at Oxford University, it is notable for being among the shorter English-language introductory [[textbook]]s in the subject, employing a terse style while also relegating a good deal of material (including a brief introduction to [[Spectrum of a ring|prime spectra]] and [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme theory]]) to the [[exercise (mathematics)|exercise]]s.

==Reviews==
Michael Berg says "this classic book, is one of the premier texts for a serious graduate (or very gifted undergraduate) student".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/introduction-to-commutative-algebra|last=Berg|first=Michael|title=Introduction to Commutative Algebra|publisher=Mathematical Association of America (MAA)|date=|access-date=2025-05-23}}</ref> [[Mark Lee Green|Mark Green]] calls it an "elegant minimalist introduction".{{sfnp|Green|1996|p=367}} W. Jonsson says "An amazing amount of information is included in the 128 pages of this book".<ref>{{cite journal|last=Jonsson|first=Wilbur|title=Introduction to Commutative algebra|journal=Canadian Mathematical Bulletin|volume=13|issue=|year=1970|page=162}}</ref>  [[Donald John Lewis|D. J. Lewis]] says "The highlight of the text is the very excellent set of problems which constitute one-third of the text".  B. R. McDonald says "The student consensus was that the text was very readable ... we were pleased with the success of the text".<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lewis|first1=D.J.|last2=McDonald|first2=B.R.|title=Introduction to Commutative Algebra|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|volume=77|issue=7|year=1970|pages=783–784}}</ref>
On the other hand, Lewis says "The text is very tersely written, examples are a bit scarce and proofs are condensed. This reviewer doubts that many students can profitably read it unassisted."

The book has enthusiastic endorsements from several math professors. Henry Pinkham, former Professor of Math at Columbia University said "probably the best introduction to Commutative Algebra, and has very good exercises."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.math.columbia.edu/department/pinkham/teaching/CommutativeAlgebra/CommutativeAlgebra.html|title=Commutative Algebra for Arithmetic and Algebraic Geometry, Math G4261, Fall 2000, Syllabus| date=21 Sep 2000 |access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref> Jonathan Wise, Associate Professor at University of Colorado Boulder says "may be the best math textbook ever written."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://math.colorado.edu/~jonathan.wise/teaching/math6150-fall-2016/ |title=Math G4261, Fall 2000, Syllabus| access-date=24 May 2025}}</ref>
